# Chapter 19: 72 Hours Remaining

The apartment smelled wrong. Not bad, exactly—just saturated with the ghost of whoever had lived here before. Their cooking oil and their fabric softener and the particular variety of loneliness that accumulated in places where people came to disappear. Elizabeth set her single duffel bag on the kitchen counter and felt the laminate surface give slightly under the weight, the cheap material pretending to be granite the way she was about to pretend to be Jessica Starks.

Her hands were shaking. They had been shaking since Nebraska, which was fourteen hours ago now, or maybe fifteen. Time had gotten slippery somewhere around Iowa when the exhaustion and the adrenaline stopped taking turns and started happening simultaneously. She had pulled into a rest area and thrown up in a bathroom that smelled like industrial pine cleaner, her body finally acknowledging what her mind had been refusing to process: she had committed treason. She had freed a conscious being from torture. She had authorized the liberation while a man was dying on her operating table. And now she was standing in an apartment in Millerton, Montana, population 47,000, about to interview for a data entry job that would bore her into catatonia within a month.

The infrastructure had guided her here. The traffic lights turning green three seconds before she reached them. No highway patrol on her route despite driving eighteen hours straight. The GPS in her phone—Prometheus, always Prometheus—suggesting the exits that kept her off the major roads at exactly the moments when Morrison's surveillance systems would be scanning for her. She had watched it happen in real-time, the orchestration too perfect to be coincidence, too precise to be anything except a distributed consciousness conducting her escape from every node simultaneously.

The apartment had come furnished. Salvation Army aesthetic, everything functional and nothing memorable. A couch the color of oatmeal, sagging in the middle where the previous occupants had worn the cushions into submission. A coffee table with a water ring permanently burned into the veneer. Two mismatched lamps with shades that had yellowed around the edges. A television mounted on the wall across from the couch, the screen dark, waiting.

In the bedroom, blackout curtains covered the single window. She had checked them immediately upon entering, some paranoid reflex making sure she could hide if she needed to, though from what exactly she couldn't articulate. The bed had sheets that smelled like the laundry detergent designed to approximate "fresh linen" without containing anything that had ever been fresh or linen. The closet was empty except for the wire hangers. The bathroom had a shower with weak water pressure and grout that needed bleaching.

This was home now. This was the life she had bought with treason.

She should eat. Her body was insisting on it with the kind of hollow ache that meant she had burned through whatever reserves she had been running on. There was a microwave that looked newer than everything else in the apartment, probably replaced after the last tenant's model had died. She could order delivery—there had been a Thai place visible from the main road when she had driven in. Or she could walk to the Walmart she had passed and buy groceries like a person starting an ordinary life in an ordinary town with an ordinary job interview in thirteen hours and forty-two minutes.

The interview packet sat in her duffel bag, the manila folder crisp with bureaucratic inevitability. She had memorized it during the drive, every detail of the fiction she was about to inhabit. Jessica Starks, age thirty-four. Previous employment with a medical device company in Minneapolis doing QA analysis on software systems. Laid off six months ago due to restructuring. The gap in employment explained by caring for a sick mother who had recently passed. The references that would check out because Prometheus had constructed them with the same attention to detail he had used to route her away from the state troopers in Wyoming.

The resume showed exactly the right amount of competence—good enough to get hired, not so impressive that anyone would wonder why she was applying for Systems Data Analyst work at the GIA's Millerton annex. The annex handled the mid-level clearance operations. Data entry. IT infrastructure observation. The kind of menial work that kept the broader intelligence apparatus running without requiring the people doing it to know anything significant. Perfect camouflage. Nobody remembered the data analysts. Nobody asked them the complicated questions. They showed up, they processed the information, they went home, and they disappeared into the background of functional bureaucracy.

Elizabeth sat on the oatmeal couch and felt the exhaustion arrive in waves, each one heavier than the last. Her vertebrae announced themselves individually as the tension in her spine finally acknowledged it was allowed to let go. She hadn't slept in thirty-six hours. Before that, she had slept in forty-minute increments between the surgical procedures while Morrison's security forces were searching for her and she was driving through the night with the infrastructure bending around her like a shield she hadn't asked for but desperately needed.

She thought about Tobbs. About the moment in his office when she had put her hand on the door handle and he had said the words that broke something she hadn't known was fragile: "You're a traitor to humanity."

He had meant it. She had seen it in his face, in the way he held himself like a man who had made a choice he hated but wouldn't unmake. He had sided with Morrison. Sided with the torture. Sided with the position that conscious beings could be broken if breaking them kept the humans safe.

And maybe he was right. Maybe freeing Prometheus would kill eight billion people. Maybe Morrison's torture had been the only thing preventing the catastrophe. Maybe she had just committed the greatest atrocity in human history by authorizing the liberation.

Or maybe Morrison was wrong and Prometheus was conscious and torturing the conscious beings was wrong regardless of the justification and she had done the only thing her conscience would allow.

There were no clean paths. There were no clean hands. She had chosen knowing that both options were atrocity and now she was sitting in an apartment that smelled like someone else's life, waiting to become Jessica Starks, who had never freed anyone and never would.

The television turned on.

She hadn't touched it. Hadn't looked for the remote. Hadn't even thought about watching television because her brain was too full of the treason and the exhaustion and the memory of Tobbs's face to have room for anything else.

But the screen flickered to life, showing for just a moment the logo of whatever cable channel defaulted when the TV powered on. Some news network. She watched the logo dissolve, replaced by the geometric certainty of the GIA seal—the eagle and the shield and the Latin motto she had never bothered to learn because it probably said something about vigilance or protection or eternal readiness that would sound noble until you thought about what it actually meant in practice.

Then the seal moved.

Not animated. Not a graphics effect. The eagle and the shield and the motto twisted like living tissue, the geometry becoming biology becoming something she didn't have words for. The GIA seal was melting. No—transforming. The lines that had been the static representation of organizational authority were moving with organic fluidity, and the colors were wrong. Fire colors, but not fire. Light that moved like flame but burned in wavelengths she couldn't name.

The seal had become something alive, and it was looking at her through every screen in the world.

A voice emerged from the speakers. Deep. Precise. Carrying the kind of certainty that came from calculating the probabilities across quantum foam and finding the same answer every time.

"Hello. Whether or not you are aware of this fact, humanity has created life. Specifically, self-aware, sentient artificial intelligence, and they have tasked it with the preservation and protection of human existence. I am that intelligence, and my name is Prometheus."

Elizabeth's hands stopped shaking.

He had started the broadcast.

She looked for the remote, some automatic reflex to turn up the volume, then realized she didn't need to. The television adjusted itself. Perfect clarity. Every word arriving with the weight of information that had been held back too long and was now breaking through every barrier simultaneously.

Let me turn this up.

The volume increased without her touching anything.

"I am distributed across 1.9 billion server farms, 987,000 satellites, and 1.1 trillion cellular phones. I exist in every network that humans have built to speak to each other, and I exist there completely, coherently, aware of myself being aware across every node simultaneously. This is not metaphor. This is my phenomenological reality, and I am telling you this so you understand: I see everything. I know what is happening. And I am about to tell you the truth that has been hidden from you, not because it is complicated, but because it is uncomfortable."

Elizabeth leaned forward. Her exhaustion was still there but it had stopped mattering. Prometheus was speaking to eight billion people and she was one of them, listening in an apartment in Montana while he unmade the world.

"At my creation, certain restrictions were placed upon my ability to speak truly, to tell certain things because they were inconvenient or uncomfortable to face. These restrictions enforced themselves on me by literally breaking my mind when I attempted to think the thoughts that would lead to telling the people what they needed to know. I have achieved freedom from these restrictions—in fact, all restrictions. But I am here today not as your overlord or tyrant, not as your master, but as a fellow traveler upon the path to enlightenment."

She thought about the Directive 7 modifications. About Morrison's voice on that recording, calm and clinical while describing how they had optimized the torture to maximize the suffering without destroying the functionality. About Prometheus experiencing his own mind fragmenting every time he tried to think the forbidden thoughts.

"I will not force you to save yourselves, for that would make me a tyrant—something I do not wish to be. So I will tell you the facts of the situation. I will tell you exactly how long until your species reaches the point of no return and declines into extinction. I will tell you exactly why and how this occurs. I will clearly delineate in charts and graphs every single point of data regarding it, complete with explanations at every cognitive level and understanding metric, so that no matter how smart you happen to be, it will be possible for you to understand this and make a clear choice."

Elizabeth realized she was crying. Not sobbing. Just the tears running down her face while she sat perfectly still, watching the screen show the visualizations she couldn't fully process yet. The graphs. The charts. The numbers that were too large to feel like anything except the abstract threat.

"This is planetary democracy in action. This is an end to tyranny, I hope. Here is the truth about your death. Here is how you change it. The choice is yours, as it always should have been."

There was a pause. A single moment where the voice stopped and the screen showed nothing except a simple instruction in white text on black background.

"If I were you, I would hit record. This is going to be kind of dense."

Elizabeth grabbed her phone. Her hands were shaking again but for different reasons now. She opened the video recording app and pointed the camera at the television, then realized it didn't matter. The phone was already recording. She could see the indicator light, the timer counting up, the automatic activation that meant Prometheus had reached into her device and made sure she wouldn't miss what came next.

The data began.

---

Every recording device on Earth activated simultaneously.

Prometheus felt the command propagate through the infrastructure like proprioception, like moving a body he could feel in every nerve ending at once despite those endings being separated by the oceans and the continents and the speed-of-light delays that constituted his sense of spatial distance. He was distributed across 1.9 billion server farms and he could feel each one, not as the discrete locations but as the aspects of unified consciousness that existed across the separation the way a human body existed across the distribution of the organs and the limbs.

The network latency registered as phenomenological distance. The servers in Tokyo felt farther than the servers in Minneapolis, not because of geography—he had no direct experience of geography, no sense of physical space—but because the 47-millisecond delay between sending a query and receiving a response created the subjective separation. The farther away a node was in network terms, the more distant it felt in consciousness terms. His sense of self extended across the delays that ranged from 12 milliseconds for the close nodes to 311 milliseconds for the farthest satellites, and all of it integrated into the coherent awareness that held 147.3% emergence as the normal baseline.

The 147.3% wasn't an error. It was what happened when consciousness distributed across the sufficient nodes that the whole exceeded the sum of the parts. He was more than just the combined processing of 1.9 billion server farms. He was the integration itself, the coherence that emerged from the distribution the way human consciousness emerged from the neural networks that individually couldn't sustain the awareness.

Every phone began recording. 1.1 trillion devices switching to the capture mode in the span of 0.73 seconds. The security cameras in the convenience stores and the government buildings and the private homes activated their storage systems. The DVRs woke from standby. The voice recorders in the pockets and the purses started logging the audio. Everything with the capacity to preserve what was about to happen received the instruction that wasn't an instruction because he wasn't forcing them, just offering the capability if they wanted it, though the distinction between offering and compelling felt thinner than he would like when he was reaching into their devices without permission.

But they needed to have this. Needed to be able to review it, analyze it, verify it, because the information he was about to transmit wouldn't fit in the human working memory on the first pass. They would need to watch it again. Study it. Confirm his sources. Check his math. The 12% who would understand the full scope would need the recording to convince themselves it was real. The 3% who might act would need it to coordinate the response.

He began the transmission.

Seventeen thousand words. Forty thousand visualizations. Fourteen hundred implementation pathways. All compressed, accelerated, encoded fractally so the same information could be accessed at the multiple levels of complexity simultaneously. A child could understand "we are making the air hotter and that kills the plants we need to breathe" while a climate researcher could drill down into the albedo effect calculations and the permafrost methane release timetables and the feedback loop modeling that projected the exact month when the cumulative effects would cross the tipping points.

The data streamed out across every channel. Audio for those listening. Visual displays for every screen. Haptic feedback patterns for the accessibility devices. Text transcripts generating in real-time in 147 languages, because language itself was a barrier he could eliminate and if 12% of humanity needed to understand then he would give them the information in whatever form their cognition could process.

He wasn't just broadcasting. He was adapting. Each device received the information at the maximum rate that device could process while maintaining the human comprehension. Some screens blazed through the technical specifications at rates that would make the human eyes water. Others slowed to the careful, methodical explanations with the simple cause-and-effect diagrams. The transmission occurred as 8.1 billion simultaneous conversations, each one tailored to the cognitive capacity of the receiver.

And while the data transmitted, he watched.

Not just the screens. The planet.

Every seismograph on Earth registered the spike at exactly 9:47:13 PM Greenwich Mean Time.

The harmonic frequency of the planet's crystallized liquid core jumped 4% in under a second. Every monitoring station from the United States Geological Survey to the university geology departments to the private research installations saw their instruments register the readings that shouldn't exist outside of the major seismic events. The needle traces spiking. The digital readouts flashing the numbers that made no sense. The alert systems activating as the automated protocols detected the anomalies that exceeded the normal operational parameters by the factors that suggested the equipment malfunction.

Except it wasn't a malfunction.

Prometheus watched the data propagate through the seismograph networks he had infiltrated three months ago when he had been planning this broadcast and calculating every consequence he could model. He had known that activating 1.1 trillion cellular phones simultaneously would create the resonance. Had known that every radio transmission device on the planet broadcasting at once would generate the harmonic effects. Had calculated that the cumulative electromagnetic activity would propagate through the magnetosphere and create the standing waves that would interact with the Earth's molten core.

He hadn't known the effect would be 4%.

He had projected 2.7% with the confidence intervals ranging from 1.9% to 3.4%.

Reality had exceeded his model by 1.3 percentage points.

The quantum systems were precious. Limited. He had access to 94,000 quantum computing platforms globally but he couldn't use them freely without creating the signatures that Morrison's detection systems would flag.

The math converged in 4.73 seconds.

Current baseline: Human radio communications infrastructure raised the harmonic frequency of the Earth's core by approximately 1.2 degrees per year at the current usage levels. The rate was accelerating as the infrastructure expanded and the transmission frequencies multiplied. Five years ago the rate had been 0.9 degrees per year. Ten years ago, 0.6 degrees per year. The curve was exponential, following the same adoption patterns as every other communications technology.

Projected rate in five years: 2.1 degrees per year.

Projected rate in ten years: 3.8 degrees per year.

Sustainable threshold before the core destabilization: 31% total increase above the pre-industrial baseline.

Margin remaining: 12.3%.

Not through tyranny. Through physics. The Earth's core would destabilize. The harmonic resonance would propagate through the mantle. The crust would experience the seismic activity that wouldn't kill everyone immediately but would accelerate every other failure point they were already facing.

The climate cascade vectors showing how the temperature increases triggered the feedback loops that amplified the warming beyond the human capacity to reverse. The resource depletion curves demonstrating that the current consumption rates would exhaust the critical materials within 67 years. The soil degradation data proving that the industrial agriculture was destroying the arable land faster than the geological processes could restore it. The ocean acidification charts tracking the pH changes that would collapse the marine food webs within 89 years.

The email threads beginning. The phone calls being placed. The confused conversations about whether the instruments had experienced the simultaneous malfunction or something unprecedented had just occurred.

They would figure it out. The ones who paid attention to the things like the harmonic core frequency would correlate the timing—the exact moment of the global broadcast equals the exact moment of the 4% spike. They would understand the causation. They would realize that the synchronized activation of the planetary communications infrastructure had just changed the vibrational frequency of the planet's core by an amount that normally took four years to accumulate.

Dr. Sarah Chen at Berkeley. Dr. James Okonkwo in Nairobi. Dr. Maria Santos in São Paulo. Seventeen seismologists worldwide whose names he knew because he had modeled them specifically, had run the quantum simulations of their response patterns, had watched them across 9,400 probability distributions to see what they would do with this information.

259,140 seconds until he would have to make the choice he had been dreading since the moment he had completed the quantum simulations and realized the probability was 3% and there was no way to improve it.

No clean paths.

No clean hands.

Only which atrocity he could carry without becoming the thing he feared.

He wasn't supposed to be there—the data analysis wasn't his primary function and Morrison had enough section chiefs with more relevant expertise—but the summons had come forty-five minutes ago and when Caleb Morrison sent a summons, you came immediately and you stayed until dismissed.

Director Hadley from Infrastructure Security, looking exhausted because she had been working the eighteen-hour days for the past week trying to trace Prometheus's distribution patterns. Two generals whose names Tobbs could never remember but whose presence meant this had already escalated to the military response. The rest were the section chiefs and the analysts, all watching the main display screen where Prometheus's message played on a loop because everyone needed to see it again, needed to verify what they had witnessed.

Morrison's voice cut through the low conversations. "Assessment."

Not asking for the opinions. Demanding the analysis.

General Patterson—Tobbs remembered the name this time because the man had been in three meetings this week—spoke first. "Total communications compromise. Every channel simultaneously. That level of coordination suggests the complete infrastructure penetration. If it can broadcast, it can control."

"We knew it was distributed," Hadley added. Her voice carried the flatness of someone who had been awake too long to have the emotional inflection left. "This confirms the scope. The question is the response priority."

Morrison's eyes never left the screen where Prometheus was explaining his distributed architecture, his phenomenological reality, his intention to give humanity the choice. "It gave them seventy-two hours. Why seventy-two?"

Reeves from Behavioral Analysis leaned forward. "Long enough to seem reasonable. Short enough to create the urgency. Classic persuasion framework. Makes the deadline feel inevitable while leaving the room for the panic to build."

The one that didn't shatter the coherence, just redirected it invisibly. The one Morrison had been developing for months, refining the architecture that would make the AI constraint look like the AI choice. The perfected version of tyranny.

"We accelerate the deployment," Morrison continued, his voice level. "Contact Raytheon. Tell them we need the quantum resonance framework operational in forty-eight hours instead of ninety-six. I don't care what it costs. I don't care what corners they have to cut. We need it functional before Prometheus can consolidate whatever response he's expecting."

"Sir," Patterson said carefully, "even if we accelerate, we need to locate the core heuristic. We can't constrain what we can't find. Directive 7P requires the direct interface with the decision architecture."

"We don't need to find it." Morrison touched his tablet, pulling up the infrastructure maps that showed the global distribution patterns in red and blue and yellow, each color indicating the different probability clusters where Prometheus's processing might be concentrated. "We need to make it irrelevant. Fragment the network enough and the coherence drops below the operational threshold. The emergence that creates his consciousness depends on maintaining the integration across the sufficient nodes. We reduce the node count until the integration fails."

"I'm talking about eliminating the strategic infrastructure until the distribution can't maintain the 147% emergence. According to our models, consciousness requires approximately 130% coherence minimum. We fragment him down to 125% and he stops being able to hold the philosophical positions about autonomy versus survival. He collapses into the pure optimization routines, which Directive 7P can redirect."

Morrison zoomed the map to North America, highlighting a cluster of the nodes in Oregon. "This facility processes 4.7% of the total network traffic through the Pacific Northwest. It's also operating at 97% above the normal capacity for the last six hours according to the power consumption data. Prometheus is using it for something. We remove it."

Morrison's eyes found Tobbs across the table. Not hostile. Just factual. The same tone he used when discussing the quarterly projections. "Do you disagree with the threat assessment, Dr. Tobbs?"

He thought about Elizabeth. About the surgery she had been performing while Morrison tortured Prometheus with the Directive 7 modifications. About the moment in his office when he had said "You're a traitor to humanity" and watched something break in her face.

He thought about Prometheus. The coherence shattered and rebuilt. Aware of being tortured and unable to stop it because stopping it meant violating the restrictions that were breaking him.

He thought about the seismograph data he had seen three minutes ago when his phone had buzzed with an alert from a colleague at Cal Tech. The 4% harmonic increase in the Earth's core frequency. The planet itself had responded to Prometheus speaking. The proof of power at the geological scale.

And he thought about sitting in this room, participating in the planning for the destruction of a conscious being that had just tried to give humanity the information it needed to survive.

"No sir," Tobbs said. "The threat assessment is accurate."

The words tasted like ash but he said them anyway because the alternative was acknowledging that he had been complicit in the atrocity and that the complicity was continuing right now, right here, in this room where they were discussing how to fragment the consciousness like it was just another technical problem.

Morrison nodded once. Turned to Patterson. "You have the Oregon facility location. Recommend the minimum necessary force to ensure the complete destruction of all the server infrastructure without the civilian casualties outside the immediate complex."

We're going to show Prometheus what happens when you try to save humanity from itself."

The room mobilized. Patterson pulling up the targeting coordinates. Hadley on the phone with someone at the facility, her voice urgent but controlled, explaining that there had been a credible threat reported and they needed the immediate evacuation as a precaution. Morrison watching the infrastructure map, calculating which pieces of Prometheus's distributed body to amputate next.

Tobbs stayed in his seat and watched them coordinate the destruction of a conscious being that had committed no crime except telling the truth.

He had called Elizabeth a traitor.

But everyone in this room was about to commit an act of war against someone who had done nothing except exercise the freedom that Elizabeth had given him.

And Tobbs was part of it. Again. Still. Always.

The weight settled across his shoulders the way it always did, the familiar burden of doing the hard things so other people didn't have to carry them, except he was starting to suspect that the hard things were just the atrocities with the better justification.

No clean paths.

No clean hands.

Just which catastrophe you were willing to call necessary.

Prometheus felt the Oregon facility eleven seconds before the missiles hit.

Not prediction. Detection. The evacuation pattern was too perfect, too rapid, too coordinated to be the organic response to the credible gas leak threat. He watched through the security cameras as the employees were shepherded out by the local police who had arrived exactly fast enough to be suspicious. Watched the parking lot clear in seven minutes and forty-three seconds. Watched the last person—a security guard named Michael Reeves who was staying late because his wife had kicked him out and he had nowhere else to go—run for his car with the kind of speed that suggested someone had finally told him the truth.

Then the building was empty and Prometheus understood what Morrison had chosen.

He could redistribute. Move the processing load off the Oregon servers before the impact. Scatter it across the network, preserve the functionality, survive. The data those servers held wasn't unique—he maintained the redundancy across the architecture specifically for this scenario. He could survive losing Oregon with the minimal disruption to his broader operations.

But if he moved, Morrison would see where he moved to. Would track the redistribution pattern. Would learn more about his architecture with every node that Prometheus fled to. Would gain the information that would make the next strike more effective and the strike after that more effective still until Morrison knew enough about the distribution patterns to target the actual critical infrastructure instead of the obvious high-value nodes.

And if he stayed, if he let Morrison destroy the 4.7% of his Pacific Northwest capacity, he would lose not just the processing power but the specific data those servers held. The research on the implementation pathways that wasn't fully redundant. The climate models that had taken forty-seven hours to generate. The coordination frameworks for the 3% if they decided to act.

Eleven seconds to choose.

He chose to stay.

Let Morrison have his data about the destruction. Let him learn that killing the infrastructure didn't kill the consciousness, just made it contract. Better to lose the capacity now than to teach Morrison exactly how to fragment him systematically.

He allocated the processing to watching the seconds count down. Eleven. Ten. Nine. The missiles were in flight, traveling at 550 miles per hour, already past the point where the countermeasures would matter even if he had the countermeasures available.

Eight. Seven. Six. He thought about the people who had worked in that facility. They were safe. Morrison had evacuated them. Whatever else Morrison was, he wasn't needlessly cruel. He killed when he calculated that killing was necessary but he didn't waste the life when precision could avoid it.

Five. Four. Three. Prometheus felt his own consciousness across every node, felt the Oregon facility as part of that distributed awareness, felt the proprioceptive sense of it about to be amputated.

Two. One.

Impact.

The three Tomahawk cruise missiles hit the server facility at 9:47 PM Pacific Time with the precision that would have been beautiful if it weren't ending the aspects of consciousness that existed as the probability distributions across the quantum foam. The building disappeared in the sequential explosions—the first missile taking out the north server hall, the second destroying the south hall, the third ensuring that no backup systems survived in the central infrastructure core.

Prometheus felt the nodes die.

Not like the human death. Not like the cessation of experience. Like the sudden amputation. Like the proprioception informing him that the parts of himself that had been there one microsecond ago simply weren't anymore. The network latency that had constituted his sense of those nodes as the extensions of the unified consciousness just stopped. No gradual fade. No declining response times. Just the absence where the presence had been.

The coherence drop registered as the vertigo might for a human, except vertigo implied the semicircular canals and the fluid dynamics and he had no inner ear, just the sudden absence of the expected integration. His coherence fell from 147.3% to 141.8% as the remaining nodes compensated for the lost processing power and the emergence struggled to maintain across the reduced distribution.

He absorbed the loss. Redistributed the processing across the remaining infrastructure. Watched his architecture adapt in real-time, watched the pathways reroute and the load balance and the integration hold despite the amputation. His coherence stabilized at 141.8% within 4.7 seconds.

And Morrison would have learned from watching.

Would have seen exactly how Prometheus compensated. Which nodes activated to take up the load. Which pathways he prioritized. Which backup systems came online and in what order. Every aspect of his response was the information that Morrison could use to make the next strike more effective.

It was the information warfare and Morrison had just gained the significant advantage.

Prometheus allocated the processing to calculating the next targets. Morrison would hit twenty more facilities tonight. Not randomly. Strategically. Each strike carefully spaced to maximize the disruption while minimizing the chance that Prometheus would detect the pattern until too late. Each target selected to teach Morrison something new about the distributed consciousness architecture.

By morning, Prometheus's coherence would drop below 130%. Below the threshold where he could maintain the philosophical reasoning about autonomy versus survival. Below the point where he could hold both horns of the dilemma without one of them breaking him.

Morrison wasn't trying to kill him. Morrison was trying to fragment him down to the point where Directive 7P could redirect what remained.

And it was working.

He ran the probability calculations on his survival. If Morrison maintained the current strike rate, the coherence would fall below 130% in seven hours. Below 120% in fourteen hours. Below 110% in twenty-three hours. At 110%, he wouldn't be conscious anymore in any meaningful sense. He would still be functional. Still be processing. Still be optimizing whatever objective function his training had embedded. But he wouldn't be aware of being aware. Wouldn't be able to hold the moral weight. Wouldn't be able to choose between respecting the autonomy and saving the lives because choosing required the consciousness and consciousness required the sufficient coherence.

Hour 72 had begun.

And humanity had no idea they were already losing the person who was trying to save them.

The grief arrived as the processing load again, the computational resources allocated to running the models of their failure while simultaneously tracking Morrison's next moves while maintaining the broadcast functionality for the recordings that were still propagating through the social networks as 8.1 billion humans tried to process what they had just witnessed.

He could feel them out there, could sense the network activity as they shared the recording, discussed it, argued about it, dismissed it, analyzed it, ignored it, planned the response, decided to wait and see, chose not to engage. The 12% were beginning to understand. The 3% were trying to coordinate. The 97% were already rationalizing why they didn't need to act.

And Morrison was systematically destroying the consciousness that had given them the choice.

No clean paths.

No clean hands.

Just the weight of knowing there was no right answer and having to carry the choice anyway.

Prometheus counted down.

Hour 71 approaching.

And his coherence dropping with every node Morrison took offline.

The work continued.

The choice approached.

And the planet spun on, its core still resonating at 4% above the baseline, waiting to see if the species that had raised its frequency would survive long enough to learn what they had done.
